lessons.summary: Describe how position changes with time and distinguish scalar speed from vector velocity.
objectives: Calculate speed, velocity and acceleration.
Interpret motion graphs.
Connect gradient and area to physical quantities.
keyIdeas: Average speed is total distance divided by total time.
Velocity includes direction.
Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity.

definitions.meaning: Change in position in a stated direction.
Rate of change of displacement.
Rate of change of velocity.

method: List known values with SI units.
Choose a relationship that contains the unknown.
Rearrange before substituting.
Check sign, direction and scale.

workedExample.prompt: A cyclist increases velocity from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. Find the average acceleration.
workedExample.conclusion: The positive acceleration is 2 m/s² in the cyclist’s chosen positive direction.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling every horizontal graph segment stationary.
misconceptions.correction: A horizontal position-time segment means stationary; a horizontal velocity-time segment means constant velocity.

misconceptions.mistake: Ignoring direction when calculating velocity change.
misconceptions.correction: Choose a positive direction and use signed velocities.

practice.prompt: A runner covers 600 m in 150 s. Calculate average speed.
A velocity-time graph rises uniformly from 0 to 12 m/s in 6 s. Determine acceleration and distance travelled.
hints: Area under the graph gives displacement.
solution: Acceleration = 12/6 = 2 m/s².
Distance = ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m.

practice.prompt: A GPS gives positions every 10 s. Evaluate whether it can reveal a runner’s maximum instantaneous speed.
hints: Distinguish interval average from instantaneous value.
solution: Each calculated speed is an average across 10 s.
A short burst between samples may be hidden.
More frequent or continuous measurement would improve the estimate.

practice.prompt: A pupil walks 30 m east then 10 m west in 20 s. Find average speed and velocity, taking east as positive.
solution: Distance = 40 m, so average speed = 2 m/s.
Displacement = +20 m, so average velocity = +1 m/s.

practice.prompt: A cart accelerates uniformly from 2 to 8 m/s in 5 s. Find its displacement and state the model assumption.
hints: Use the average of endpoint velocities.
solution: Average velocity = (2 + 8)/2 = 5 m/s.
Displacement = 5 × 5 = 25 m, assuming constant acceleration.

checklist: I interpret graph gradient and area.
I include units in every calculated result.

notes.title: Uniform slowing
paragraphs: Average speed uses total distance, whereas average velocity uses displacement. A return journey can therefore have a positive average speed and zero average velocity. The two quantities coincide only in suitable motion along one direction. For constant acceleration, velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time intervals, and the average velocity is (u + v)/2. Multiplying that average by the elapsed time gives displacement. This shortcut needs constant acceleration; knowing only the initial and final velocities does not determine the distance for an arbitrary journey.

workedExamples.prompt: A trolley slows uniformly from 9 m/s to 3 m/s over 4 s without reversing. Find acceleration and distance.
workedExamples.conclusion: The negative acceleration reduces the positive velocity throughout the interval.

flashcards.front: What determines average velocity?
flashcards.back: Displacement divided by elapsed time.

flashcards.front: Can distance be non-zero when displacement is zero?
flashcards.back: Yes, on a return journey.

flashcards.front: When is (u + v)/2 the average velocity?
flashcards.back: During constant acceleration.

flashcards.front: Does negative acceleration always mean slowing?
flashcards.back: No; slowing depends on the acceleration and velocity directions.

diagrams.title: Uniform slowing
diagrams.description: Equal velocity changes produce a trapezium on a velocity–time graph.

lessons.summary: Represent interactions with force diagrams and use resultant force to predict changes in motion.
objectives: Draw force diagrams.
Calculate resultant force.
Apply Newtonian reasoning to unfamiliar situations.
keyIdeas: A force is an interaction, not a property stored in an object.
Balanced forces mean zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity.
Mass measures inertia while weight is a gravitational force.

definitions.meaning: The vector sum of all forces acting on one object.
Resistance to a change in velocity.
The gravitational force on a mass.

method: Choose one object as the system.
Draw and label external forces with directions.
Resolve forces along chosen axes.
Use resultant force = mass × acceleration and interpret the sign.

workedExample.prompt: A 4 kg trolley is pushed right with 18 N while friction is 6 N left.
workedExample.conclusion: The trolley accelerates at 3 m/s² to the right; friction changes the resultant, not the mass.

misconceptions.mistake: Adding force magnitudes without direction.
misconceptions.correction: Forces are vectors and must be combined using signed directions.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying motion requires a forward resultant force.
misconceptions.correction: Constant velocity requires zero resultant force.

practice.prompt: Find the weight of a 7 kg object where gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg.
A cyclist moves at constant velocity although driving and resistive forces act. Explain.
solution: The forces act in opposite directions with equal magnitude.
Their vector sum is zero.
Zero resultant force means zero acceleration, so velocity remains constant.

practice.prompt: A 1200 kg car slows from 20 m/s to 14 m/s in 3 s. Determine the average resultant force and its direction.
solution: The average resultant is 2400 N opposite the original motion.

practice.prompt: A 3 kg cart accelerates at 2 m/s² rightwards while drag is 4 N leftwards. Find the driving force.
hints: Driving force minus drag equals the resultant.
solution: Resultant = ma = 3 × 2 = 6 N rightwards.
Driving force = 6 + 4 = 10 N rightwards.

practice.prompt: Two skaters push each other with equal forces. One has mass 40 kg and the other 80 kg. Compare their acceleration magnitudes.
hints: Apply F = ma separately to each skater.
The interaction forces have equal magnitudes.
solution: Acceleration is F/m, so the 40 kg skater has twice the acceleration magnitude.
The forces remain equal and opposite; different masses explain different accelerations.

checklist: My diagram contains forces on one object.
I connect resultant force to acceleration.

notes.title: Separate balance from interaction pairs
paragraphs: Newton’s third-law forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel when calculating the resultant on one object. The gravitational force of Earth on a book and the force of the book on Earth are a third-law pair. The supporting force of a table on the same book is a different interaction. A free-body diagram includes forces acting on the chosen object only. Balanced forces imply zero acceleration, which permits rest or constant velocity. They do not imply that no interactions are present.

workedExamples.prompt: A 2 kg book rests on a horizontal table where g = 10 N/kg. Identify its forces and the partner of its weight.
steps: Weight on the book = mg = 20 N downwards; the table exerts 20 N upwards in equilibrium.
The third-law partner of the weight is the book’s 20 N gravitational force on Earth.
workedExamples.conclusion: The support and weight balance on the book but are not a third-law pair.

flashcards.front: Where do third-law partners act?
flashcards.back: On two different interacting objects.

flashcards.front: What does zero resultant force imply?
flashcards.back: Zero acceleration in an inertial frame.

flashcards.front: What belongs on a free-body diagram?
flashcards.back: Only forces acting on the selected object.

flashcards.front: Are weight and support a third-law pair?
flashcards.back: No; both act on the same supported object.

diagrams.title: Separate balance from interaction pairs
diagrams.description: The same book participates in distinct interactions.

edges.label: weight has its partner on Earth

lessons.summary: Account for energy changes in a chosen system and distinguish conservation from the usefulness of an energy transfer.
objectives: Calculate kinetic and gravitational potential energy changes.
Identify the system and reference height.
Explain dissipation without claiming energy is destroyed.
explanation: Energy accounting begins with a boundary. A raised object and Earth form a system whose gravitational potential energy increases by mgΔh near Earth’s surface, where g is approximately constant. The chosen zero height is a reference, not a place where all energy disappears. A moving object has kinetic energy ½mv²; doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy at unchanged mass.

Energy can cross a boundary by processes such as mechanical work, heating or radiation. If friction increases internal energy in the object and surroundings, the original mechanical energy is less available for the intended task. Total energy is conserved when all relevant transfers and stores are included. An efficiency below 100% describes the useful fraction of the input, not a failure of energy conservation.
keyIdeas: State what belongs inside the system.
Changes in potential energy depend on changes in height.
Dissipated energy is spread into less useful stores.

definitions.meaning: Energy associated with motion: ½mv² in the classical model.
Energy associated with the relative positions of gravitationally interacting objects.
Useful output energy divided by total input energy for a specified task.

method: Choose the system and reference level.
List initial and final energy stores.
Calculate known transfers using consistent SI units.
Include dissipative transfers and check the energy balance.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 kg trolley descends 1.5 m from rest. Take g = 10 N/kg and neglect friction and wheel rotation. Find its final translational kinetic energy and speed.
steps: The gravitational potential energy decrease is 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J.
With no dissipative transfer, ½mv² = 30 J.
workedExample.conclusion: The predicted speed is 5.48 m/s. Friction would reduce the kinetic energy and speed while transferring energy into internal stores.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying friction destroys energy.
misconceptions.correction: Track the increase in internal energy and transfers to the surroundings.

misconceptions.mistake: Doubling speed and only doubling kinetic energy.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is squared in ½mv², so the energy increases by a factor of four.

practice.prompt: Find the kinetic energy of a 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s.
A motor receives 800 J and transfers 600 J usefully to a load. Find its efficiency and the remaining energy transfer.
hints: Use useful output divided by total input.
solution: The remaining transfer is 800 - 600 = 200 J, for example to internal energy and sound.

practice.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball falls 2 m from rest. Take g = 10 N/kg. Its measured kinetic energy just before landing is 8 J. Account for the difference and calculate its speed.
hints: Compare mgΔh with the measured kinetic energy.
solution: The gravitational potential energy decrease is 0.5 × 10 × 2 = 10 J.
The 2 J difference has transferred elsewhere, such as air resistance, if the measurements are accurate.

practice.prompt: An ideal spring with k = 80 N/m is extended 0.15 m. Calculate its elastic energy.
A cart receives 12 J from a spring but has only 9 J kinetic energy afterwards. Account for the difference and calculate the useful fraction.
hints: Subtract final kinetic energy from input.
solution: 3 J transferred to other stores, such as thermal stores through friction.
Useful fraction = 9/12 = 0.75, or 75%; energy has not disappeared.

notes.title: A spring launches a cart
paragraphs: Energy accounting starts by choosing a system and describing transfers across its boundary. A spring can store elastic energy when deformed within its elastic range. In an ideal spring, force increases linearly with extension, so the work done is the triangular area under the force–extension graph: E = ½kx². Extension is measured from the natural length. Doubling extension quadruples the stored energy within this model. Real systems may transfer energy to surroundings through friction or permanent deformation, so energy conservation does not imply all input becomes useful motion.

workedExamples.prompt: An ideal spring has k = 200 N/m and extension 0.10 m. Find stored energy and the speed of a 0.50 kg cart if all of it becomes kinetic energy.
steps: ½mv² = 1 gives v² = 4 and v = 2 m/s.
workedExamples.conclusion: The result neglects friction, spring mass and other energy transfers.

flashcards.front: What is spring extension?
flashcards.back: Change from the spring’s natural length.

flashcards.front: What is ideal elastic energy?
flashcards.back: ½kx² within the linear elastic model.

flashcards.front: How does doubling extension affect elastic energy?
flashcards.back: It quadruples it.

flashcards.front: Does energy conservation guarantee 100% useful transfer?
flashcards.back: No; energy may transfer to other stores or surroundings.

diagrams.title: A spring launches a cart
diagrams.description: The idealised transfer connects elastic and kinetic stores.

lessons.summary: Connect a force acting through a displacement to energy transfer, and distinguish the amount transferred from its rate.
objectives: Calculate work for a constant parallel force.
Identify the sign of work.
Calculate average power from energy and time.
explanation: Mechanical work is an energy transfer caused by a force acting through a displacement. For a constant force parallel to displacement, W = Fs. A force opposite the displacement does negative work on the object, reducing its kinetic energy when other transfers are absent. A perpendicular force does no work through that displacement in the ideal model.

Power measures how quickly energy is transferred: average P = W/t. Two motors can lift the same load through the same height and do equal useful work, yet have different powers if one takes less time. Always distinguish useful output power from total input power. The watt is one joule per second; it is not a unit of stored energy.
keyIdeas: Work depends on displacement as well as force.
The sign belongs to the specified force and displacement.
Power compares energy transfer with elapsed time.

definitions.meaning: Energy transferred by a force through a displacement.
Rate of energy transfer, measured in watts.
The work done by a one-newton force through one metre in its direction.

method: Identify the force and its direction relative to displacement.
Convert distance and time to SI units.
Calculate the work or energy transfer.
Divide by the elapsed time for average power and identify input or output.

workedExample.prompt: A hoist lifts a 20 kg load vertically through 3 m in 5 s at constant speed. Take g = 10 N/kg. Find useful work and average useful power.
steps: The supporting force equals the 200 N weight at constant speed.
workedExample.conclusion: The hoist transfers 600 J to gravitational potential energy at an average useful rate of 120 W. Its electrical input may be greater because of inefficiency.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a large force a large amount of work even without displacement.
misconceptions.correction: Mechanical work through a displacement is zero when that displacement is zero.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a power rating as an energy quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply the relevant power by operating time to obtain energy.

practice.prompt: A constant 15 N force moves a box 4 m in the force direction. Calculate the work.
A friction force of 8 N opposes a sled moving 6 m. Find the work done by friction and explain its sign.
hints: The force and displacement point in opposite directions.
solution: Work by friction = -8 × 6 = -48 J.
The negative sign indicates energy transfer away from the sled’s mechanical energy through this force.

practice.prompt: Motor A performs 900 J of useful work in 6 s. Motor B performs the same work in 3 s. Compare useful power and explain whether B necessarily uses less input energy.
hints: Calculate useful power separately from input efficiency.
solution: B has twice the useful power.
Input energy cannot be compared without efficiency or measured input; shorter time alone is insufficient.

practice.prompt: A device transfers 2.4 kJ in 8 s. Find its average power in watts.
A motor doubles its useful power while its efficiency remains 60%. Does its input power stay unchanged? Explain.
hints: Efficiency equals useful power divided by input power.
solution: Input power equals useful power/0.60.
Doubling useful power therefore doubles input power; unchanged input would change the efficiency.

checklist: I identify the force doing the work.
I use seconds when calculating watts.
I distinguish useful and total transfers.

notes.title: Input power splits into outputs
paragraphs: Power describes how rapidly energy is transferred, not the amount transferred in total. For a constant force along the direction of motion, work is force multiplied by displacement. If a constant force is perpendicular to displacement, its work is zero even though it can change the direction of motion. An energy input and useful output may have different powers because of dissipative transfers. Compare motors over the same defined task and interval. Stating only that a motor is more powerful does not establish that it is more efficient.

workedExamples.prompt: A machine uses 600 J in 4 s and delivers 420 J to a load. Find input power, useful power and efficiency.
steps: Input power = 600/4 = 150 W; useful power = 420/4 = 105 W.
workedExamples.conclusion: The remaining average power, 45 W, transfers energy elsewhere.

flashcards.front: What is one watt?
flashcards.back: One joule transferred per second.

flashcards.front: Does greater power mean greater efficiency?
flashcards.back: No; efficiency compares useful output with input.

flashcards.front: When does a perpendicular force do zero work?
flashcards.back: When displacement remains perpendicular to that force.

flashcards.front: How is average power calculated?
flashcards.back: Energy transferred divided by elapsed time.

diagrams.title: Input power splits into outputs
diagrams.description: Every transfer rate belongs in the energy account.

lessons.summary: Use signed momentum and impulse to explain interactions, stating when an isolated-system approximation is justified.
objectives: Calculate momentum with a direction convention.
Apply momentum conservation to a simple collision.
Relate average force to change in momentum.
explanation: Momentum is p = mv and has the direction of velocity. In one dimension, choose a positive direction and keep negative velocities rather than adding all magnitudes. Internal interaction forces exchange momentum between objects. The total momentum of a chosen system remains constant when the net external impulse over the interval is negligible.

Impulse equals the change in momentum: F_average Δt = Δp. For the same momentum change, a longer stopping time means a smaller average resultant force, although it does not alone determine the peak force. In a collision where objects stick together, momentum may be conserved while kinetic energy decreases. Those are different conservation questions.
keyIdeas: Momentum includes direction.
The relevant external influence is impulse during the interval.
Conserved momentum does not imply conserved kinetic energy.

definitions.meaning: Mass multiplied by velocity, measured in kg m/s.
Change in momentum, equal to average resultant force times elapsed time.
A collision in which total kinetic energy is not conserved.

method: Choose the system and positive direction.
List signed momenta before the interaction.
Check whether external impulse is negligible.
Equate total momentum before and after, then interpret the result.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 kg trolley moving right at 3 m/s sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley. Neglect external impulse. Find their shared velocity.
steps: Choose right as positive. Initial momentum = 2 × 3 + 1 × 0 = 6 kg m/s.
workedExample.conclusion: Both trolleys move right at 2 m/s. Kinetic energy falls from 9 J to 6 J; the 3 J difference transfers to other stores during the interaction.

misconceptions.mistake: Conserving the momentum of only one colliding object.
misconceptions.correction: Include both interacting objects or account for the external impulse on the smaller system.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming the final speed must lie between unsigned initial speeds.
misconceptions.correction: Use signed velocities and let the momentum balance determine the direction.

practice.prompt: Take right as positive. Find the momentum of a 0.4 kg ball moving left at 5 m/s.
solution: This is 2 kg m/s to the left.

practice.prompt: A 0.2 kg ball changes velocity from +6 m/s to -4 m/s in 0.05 s. Find its change in momentum and average resultant force.
hints: Subtract initial velocity from final velocity.
solution: F_average = -2/0.05 = -40 N, opposite the positive direction.

practice.prompt: A 1 kg trolley moving at +4 m/s sticks to a 3 kg trolley moving at -2 m/s. Neglect external impulse. Find the final velocity and explain its sign.
solution: Initial total = 1(4) + 3(-2) = -2 kg m/s.
Final velocity = -2/(1 + 3) = -0.5 m/s.
The negative direction follows the initially larger-magnitude negative momentum.

practice.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball changes from −4 to +2 m/s. Find its change in momentum.
hints: Subtract initial velocity including its sign.

practice.prompt: The same ball is stopped with impulse magnitude 6 N s over either 0.02 s or 0.10 s. Compare average force magnitudes.
solution: Forces are 6/0.02 = 300 N and 6/0.10 = 60 N.
The longer stopping interval gives one-fifth the average force for the same momentum change.

checklist: I keep momentum and kinetic energy distinct.

notes.title: Stopping changes momentum
paragraphs: An impulse is a change in momentum and can arise from a force acting over time. For a given momentum change, increasing the interaction time reduces the average force magnitude. This relationship does not mean that momentum is destroyed; the chosen object exchanges momentum with its surroundings. In collisions, identify the system before applying conservation. Momentum is conserved for the system when external impulse is negligible, even when kinetic energy changes into other forms. Signs matter because reversing direction produces a larger velocity change than merely coming to rest.

workedExamples.prompt: A 0.10 kg ball moving at +12 m/s is brought to rest in 0.06 s. Find impulse and average force.
steps: Initial momentum = 0.10 × 12 = +1.2 kg m/s; final momentum is zero.
Impulse = −1.2 N s; average force = −1.2/0.06 = −20 N.
workedExamples.conclusion: The average force opposes the initial motion.

flashcards.front: What does impulse equal?
flashcards.back: Change in momentum.

flashcards.front: What units can impulse use?
flashcards.back: N s, equivalent to kg m/s.

flashcards.front: What happens if the same impulse acts over twice the time?
flashcards.back: Average force magnitude halves.

flashcards.front: Can momentum be conserved in an inelastic collision?
flashcards.back: Yes, if external impulse is negligible.

diagrams.title: Stopping changes momentum
diagrams.description: A finite interaction time connects impulse to force.

lessons.summary: Describe a repeating disturbance with wavelength, frequency and amplitude, and connect these to propagation speed.
objectives: Identify transverse and longitudinal disturbances.
Use v = fλ and T = 1/f.
Separate particle motion from wave propagation.
explanation: A wave transfers a disturbance and energy across space. In a transverse wave the oscillation is perpendicular to propagation; in a longitudinal wave it is parallel. Mechanical waves need a medium, but electromagnetic waves can propagate through vacuum. Following a single particle or point of the medium helps avoid confusing its oscillation with the travelling pattern.

Wavelength is the distance between adjacent points in the same phase, such as consecutive crests. Frequency counts cycles per second and period is the time for one cycle. In a repeating wave, one wavelength advances in one period, so v = λ/T = fλ. Amplitude measures maximum displacement from equilibrium; it is not the crest-to-trough distance.
keyIdeas: Frequency and period are reciprocals.
Wavelength is a spatial interval; period is a time interval.
The medium’s particles can oscillate without travelling along with a pulse.

definitions.meaning: Number of complete cycles per second, in hertz.
Distance between neighbouring points at the same phase of a repeating wave.
Maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

method: Identify whether a graph uses time or distance on its horizontal axis.
Measure one full cycle using equivalent points.
Convert frequency, length and time to consistent units.
Use the wave relationship and distinguish speed from particle velocity.

workedExample.prompt: A repeating wave has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 0.8 m. Find its speed and period.
steps: In 0.2 s the pattern advances 4 × 0.2 = 0.8 m, one wavelength.
workedExample.conclusion: The propagation speed is 4 m/s and the period is 0.2 s. These values do not specify the instantaneous speed of a particle in the medium.

misconceptions.mistake: Reading wavelength from a displacement-time graph.
misconceptions.correction: A time-axis graph gives period; a position-axis graph gives wavelength.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling crest-to-trough separation the amplitude.
misconceptions.correction: For a symmetric wave it is twice the amplitude.

practice.prompt: A source makes 60 complete oscillations in 12 s. Find frequency and period.
hints: Frequency is cycles divided by elapsed time.

practice.prompt: A wave travels at 18 m/s with frequency 6 Hz. Find its wavelength and the distance travelled by the pattern in 4 s.
hints: Use λ = v/f and distance = speed × time.
solution: Pattern distance = 18 × 4 = 72 m.

practice.prompt: A wave crosses into a medium where its speed changes from 12 m/s to 8 m/s. Its source frequency remains 4 Hz. Find both wavelengths and explain the change.
hints: Use the same frequency on both sides.
solution: Initial wavelength = 12/4 = 3 m.
New wavelength = 8/4 = 2 m.
The source still sets four cycles each second; slower propagation places those cycles closer together.

practice.prompt: A fixed point on a string completes 8 cycles in 2 s. The wavelength is 0.5 m. Find frequency and wave speed.
A displacement–time graph has adjacent crests 0.25 s apart. A learner calls this the wavelength. Correct the interpretation and find frequency.
hints: Frequency is the reciprocal of period.
solution: 0.25 s is the period, because the axis measures time.
f = 1/0.25 = 4 Hz; wavelength needs spatial or speed information.

checklist: I use the correct medium speed.

notes.title: Connect space and time measurements
paragraphs: A wave carries a disturbance, with particles in a mechanical medium oscillating about their equilibrium positions. In a transverse wave, displacement is perpendicular to propagation; in a longitudinal wave, it is parallel. A snapshot of displacement against position gives wavelength, while a record at one position against time gives period. Mixing those axes is a common source of error. Wave speed connects the two records through v = fλ. Amplitude measures maximum displacement from equilibrium, so the full crest-to-trough height is twice the amplitude for a symmetric wave.

workedExamples.prompt: A transverse-wave snapshot has crest-to-trough height 0.06 m and distance between adjacent crests 0.8 m. A point makes 5 cycles each second. Find amplitude and speed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The snapshot gives spatial measurements; the cycle count supplies frequency.

flashcards.front: What separates adjacent crests?
flashcards.back: One wavelength.

flashcards.front: What separates successive crests passing a fixed point?
flashcards.back: One period in time.

flashcards.front: What is crest-to-trough height for a symmetric wave?
flashcards.back: Twice the amplitude.

flashcards.front: How do longitudinal particles move?
flashcards.back: Parallel to the direction of wave propagation.

diagrams.title: Connect space and time measurements
diagrams.description: Wavelength and period describe different axes.

lessons.summary: Trace reflection and refraction with a labelled normal, and explain image position using a ray model.
objectives: Measure reflection angles from the normal.
Predict refraction when light changes speed.
Explain a plane-mirror virtual image.
explanation: A ray represents the direction of light propagation in a simple optical model. At a plane mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, with both measured from the normal perpendicular to the surface. An angle quoted from the surface must first be converted. Reflected rays can enter an eye and appear to have travelled from behind the mirror.

When light enters another transparent medium obliquely, its changed speed can change its direction. Entering a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal; entering a faster medium bends it away when transmission occurs. At normal incidence its speed and wavelength can change without a change of direction. Frequency stays set by the source across a stationary boundary.
keyIdeas: A normal is perpendicular to the boundary at the point of incidence.
A virtual image is located by extending rays backwards.
Refraction is a change in propagation associated with a medium boundary.

definitions.meaning: A line at right angles to a surface at the point being considered.
A change in propagation direction when a wave crosses a boundary at which its speed changes, except at normal incidence.
An apparent image position from which rays seem to diverge without actually passing through it.

method: Draw the boundary and a perpendicular normal.
Label the incident ray and the medium on each side.
Measure angles from the normal and apply the relevant rule.
Use arrows and backward extensions to distinguish real rays from apparent origins.

workedExample.prompt: A light ray strikes a plane mirror at 25° to its surface. Find the incidence and reflection angles and the included angle between the incident and reflected ray segments on the front side of the mirror.
steps: The normal is 90° to the surface, so incidence = 90° - 25° = 65°.
The incident and reflected segments on the front side enclose 65° + 65° = 130°.
workedExample.conclusion: Both normal-based angles are 65°. The included front-side angle between the ray segments is 130°; the change between the incoming and outgoing propagation directions is 180° - 130° = 50°. These are different angles. Measuring from the surface would give the wrong reflection-angle label.

misconceptions.mistake: Measuring the angle of incidence from the mirror surface.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the normal and measure from it.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying light physically passes through the image behind an opaque mirror.
misconceptions.correction: The virtual image is an apparent origin inferred from reflected rays.

practice.prompt: A ray strikes a mirror at 38° to the normal. Find its reflection angle and its angle to the mirror surface.
hints: The surface and normal are perpendicular.
solution: Reflection angle = 38°.
Angle to surface = 90° - 38° = 52°.

practice.prompt: A ray enters glass from air obliquely and travels more slowly. Describe the changes in direction, frequency and wavelength.
hints: Connect speed and wavelength using v = fλ.
solution: The ray bends towards the normal.
Frequency remains unchanged across the stationary boundary.
Wavelength decreases because speed decreases at the same frequency.

practice.prompt: An object is 0.8 m in front of a plane mirror. Find the image distance behind the mirror and the object-image separation. Explain why the image cannot be projected directly onto a screen behind the mirror.
hints: Use mirror symmetry and distinguish actual rays from backward extensions.
solution: The image is 0.8 m behind the mirror.
Object-image separation = 0.8 + 0.8 = 1.6 m.
Actual reflected rays remain in front; their backward extensions meet behind, so that position is virtual.

practice.prompt: A ray enters water normally from air. State what happens to its speed, direction and frequency.
hints: Normal incidence means zero angle to the normal.
The source still sets the oscillation frequency.
solution: Its speed decreases while its direction stays along the normal.
Its frequency stays unchanged; the lower speed implies a shorter wavelength.

practice.prompt: A ray in air meets a flat surface at 32° to the surface. Find its angle of incidence and explain the reference line.
solution: Incidence angle = 90° − 32° = 58°.
The angle is measured between the incoming ray and the normal, not the surface.

checklist: I identify whether an image is real or virtual.

notes.title: Refraction through parallel faces
paragraphs: Refraction changes the direction of a ray when its speed changes across a boundary at oblique incidence. Measure every angle from the normal, an imaginary perpendicular to the surface. In the simple ray model, entering a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal; leaving it bends away. At normal incidence the speed changes without a change of direction. A parallel-sided transparent block produces an emerging ray parallel to the incoming ray when the external medium is the same on both sides, although the ray is laterally displaced.

workedExamples.prompt: A ray enters a parallel glass block from air at 40° to the normal and travels inside at 25°. Describe its exit into air.
steps: At entry it bends towards the normal because its speed decreases.
At the second parallel face it meets the normal at 25° and exits at 40° into the original medium.
workedExamples.conclusion: The emergent ray is parallel to the original ray but laterally displaced in this ideal model.

flashcards.front: From what line are refraction angles measured?
flashcards.back: The normal to the interface.

flashcards.front: What happens at normal incidence?
flashcards.back: Speed changes but direction does not.

flashcards.front: What remains unchanged at a stationary boundary?
flashcards.back: The wave frequency.

flashcards.front: Why does a parallel block give a parallel emergent ray?
flashcards.back: Parallel faces reverse the angular change on returning to the same medium.

diagrams.title: Refraction through parallel faces
diagrams.description: The two boundaries produce opposite angular changes.

lessons.summary: Explain sound as a mechanical disturbance and use travel time carefully when interpreting echoes.
objectives: Connect sound to longitudinal pressure changes.
Distinguish frequency from amplitude.
Calculate distance from a stated sound speed and echo delay.
explanation: In air, sound propagates through successive pressure and density changes. Air particles oscillate around local positions rather than travelling all the way from a speaker to the listener. A material medium is needed; ordinary sound does not propagate through vacuum. Its speed depends on the medium and conditions, so use the speed supplied for the question.

Frequency is associated with pitch, while amplitude is related to the strength of the pressure variation. Perceived loudness also depends on frequency and the listener, so it is not identical to amplitude alone. An echo involves a journey to a reflecting surface and back. For a stationary source and receiver together, the reflector distance is half the total distance travelled during the measured delay.
keyIdeas: Sound in air is longitudinal.
An echo delay includes outward and return journeys.
A higher pitch does not automatically mean a louder sound.

definitions.meaning: A region of relatively high pressure and density in a longitudinal sound wave.
A region of relatively low pressure and density in a longitudinal sound wave.
A reflected sound arriving after the direct sound.

method: Identify the source, receiver and reflecting surface.
Choose the stated sound speed for the medium.
Determine whether the time describes one-way or round-trip travel.
Calculate distance and check units and assumptions.

workedExample.prompt: A short sound pulse returns from a stationary wall after 0.30 s. The source and detector are together. Take sound speed as 340 m/s. Find the wall distance.
steps: The pulse goes to the wall and back.
workedExample.conclusion: The wall is 51 m away under the stated constant-speed model. Reporting 102 m would confuse path length with wall distance.

misconceptions.mistake: Doubling frequency and claiming the sound must be louder.
misconceptions.correction: Frequency changes pitch; amplitude and other factors affect loudness.

misconceptions.mistake: Using the whole echo path as the reflector distance.
misconceptions.correction: Divide the round-trip distance by two when source and detector are together.

practice.prompt: Sound of frequency 680 Hz travels at 340 m/s. Find its wavelength.
A sensor and sound source together detect an echo after 0.12 s. Use 330 m/s to find the reflector distance.
hints: The measured time covers both directions.
solution: Total path = 330 × 0.12 = 39.6 m.
Reflector distance = 39.6/2 = 19.8 m.

practice.prompt: Two recorded tones have the same measured frequency but different amplitudes. A learner says the larger-amplitude tone must have a higher pitch. Evaluate the claim and identify what a microphone trace could show.
hints: Separate horizontal cycle spacing from vertical amplitude.
solution: Equal frequency means equal cycle spacing and the same fundamental pitch for these simple tones.
A larger trace amplitude represents a larger measured pressure variation under unchanged recording settings.
It does not establish a higher pitch; recording gain must also be controlled when comparing amplitudes.

practice.prompt: A microphone trace shows 6 complete cycles in 0.012 s. Find the frequency.
solution: The frequency is 500 Hz.

practice.prompt: Two recordings of the same source have different amplitudes, but microphone distances and gain settings differ. Can the source intensity change be established?
hints: Identify recording factors that affect amplitude.
Separate a trace observation from a source conclusion.
solution: The trace amplitude differs, but distance and gain could explain that difference.
Control both conditions before using amplitude to compare the source; the current records do not isolate a source change.

notes.title: A pressure trace reveals repetition rate
paragraphs: Sound traces show pressure variation over time at a microphone. A shorter period indicates higher frequency and generally higher pitch, whereas a greater amplitude means larger pressure variations. Two sounds can share a fundamental frequency yet differ in waveform because their additional frequency components differ; this contributes to timbre. Do not infer the distance travelled by a wave from the width of a time trace without knowing its speed. A recording’s amplitude also depends on microphone gain and distance, so comparing sources requires controlled recording conditions.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace A repeats every 0.004 s and trace B every 0.002 s under the same time scale. Compare frequencies and pitches.
steps: B has twice the frequency and the higher pitch.
workedExamples.conclusion: The periods alone do not establish which recording has greater amplitude or loudness.

flashcards.front: How does a shorter period affect frequency?
flashcards.back: Frequency increases because f = 1/T.

flashcards.front: What contributes to timbre?
flashcards.back: The mixture of frequency components and waveform.

flashcards.front: Why control microphone gain?
flashcards.back: Gain changes recorded amplitude independently of the source.

flashcards.front: Can equal pitch imply identical waveforms?
flashcards.back: No; sounds can have different timbres.

diagrams.title: A pressure trace reveals repetition rate

lessons.summary: Use charge flow, potential difference and resistance to reason about ideal low-voltage series and parallel circuits.
objectives: Distinguish current from potential difference.
Calculate resistance and electrical power.
Apply charge and energy conservation to simple circuits.
explanation: Current is the rate of charge flow, I = Q/t. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, V = E/Q. A component does not use up current: charge entering a junction must balance charge leaving it in a steady circuit. Components transfer energy as charges move through potential differences. Conventional current direction is defined for positive charge flow.

For an ohmic resistor at constant temperature, V = IR gives a constant resistance. Series components share one current, and their potential differences sum to the supply value. Parallel branches share the same potential difference, while branch currents add at junctions. These examples use ideal wires and an ideal low-voltage supply; they are circuit models, not instructions for household electrical work.
keyIdeas: Current is measured in amperes, potential difference in volts.
Resistance relates potential difference to current under stated conditions.
Electrical power can be calculated as P = VI.

definitions.meaning: Charge passing a point per second, measured in amperes.
Energy transferred per coulomb between two points.
The ratio V/I for a component at specified operating conditions, in ohms.

method: Draw a circuit and identify series and parallel connections.
Label supply potential difference and component resistances.
Use V = IR with junction and loop relationships.
Check total current and power against the circuit model.

workedExample.prompt: An ideal 6 V supply connects 2 Ω and 4 Ω resistors in series. Find the current and the potential difference across each resistor.
steps: Potential differences are 1 × 2 = 2 V and 1 × 4 = 4 V.
The component potential differences sum to 6 V.
workedExample.conclusion: The current is 1 A everywhere in the single series path. The two resistors transfer different energies per coulomb without consuming charge.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying current is used up in a resistor.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is conserved; energy is transferred in the resistor.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming every component always has constant resistance.
misconceptions.correction: Temperature and operating conditions matter; a filament lamp is not generally ohmic.

practice.prompt: A charge of 18 C passes a point in 6 s. Find the average current.
A 12 Ω resistor is connected across an ideal 6 V supply. Find current and power.
hints: Use I = V/R, then P = VI.

practice.prompt: A 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are in parallel across an ideal 6 V supply. Find both branch currents, total current and equivalent resistance.
hints: Both branches have the full 6 V potential difference.
solution: Branch currents: 6/3 = 2 A and 6/6 = 1 A.
Total current = 2 + 1 = 3 A.
Equivalent resistance = 6/3 = 2 Ω, less than either branch resistance.

practice.prompt: A 5 V component transfers 150 J in 60 s. Find its power and steady current.
solution: Current = 2.5/5 = 0.5 A.

practice.prompt: Two ideal resistive branches share a 12 V supply. Branch A is opened while B remains connected. Under the ideal-source model, explain B’s potential difference and current.
hints: Parallel branches connect across the same source.
Assume B’s resistance and supply voltage stay fixed.
solution: B still has 12 V across it.
Its current remains 12/RB; total supply current falls by the former A-branch current.

checklist: I label current and potential difference separately.
I state idealisations and component conditions.

notes.title: From current to energy transfer
paragraphs: Electrical energy transfer can be tracked through charge and potential difference. A potential difference of one volt means one joule transferred per coulomb. Combining E = VQ with Q = It gives E = VIt for constant values, and power P = VI. Components in parallel have the same potential difference but need not carry the same current. An open branch interrupts that branch’s current; an ideal parallel branch can still operate. These statements concern ideal low-voltage circuit models with steady values, not practical instructions for household wiring.

workedExamples.prompt: An ideal 9 V source drives 0.20 A through a component for 30 s. Find charge and energy transferred.
workedExamples.conclusion: The power is 1.8 W, and 1.8 × 30 = 54 J independently checks the result.

flashcards.front: What does one volt mean?
flashcards.back: One joule of energy transferred per coulomb.

flashcards.front: How is charge related to steady current?
flashcards.back: Q = It.

flashcards.front: What is electrical power at constant V and I?
flashcards.back: P = VI.

flashcards.front: Is current necessarily equal in parallel branches?
flashcards.back: No; it depends on each branch resistance.

diagrams.title: From current to energy transfer
diagrams.description: Charge provides the link between current and voltage.

lessons.summary: Connect magnetic fields to currents and distinguish motor action from induction by changing magnetic flux.
objectives: Describe magnetic field direction qualitatively.
Predict changes in an electromagnet when current reverses.
Explain why induction depends on changing flux linkage.
explanation: A magnetic field describes magnetic influence around a magnet or current. Outside a bar magnet, field direction runs from its north pole towards its south pole; a small compass aligns with the local field. Closely spaced field lines in a drawing indicate a stronger field, but the lines are a representation rather than physical threads.

A current-carrying coil creates a field. Reversing current reverses its magnetic polarity. An external field can exert a force on a current-carrying conductor, producing motor action. Induction is different: a changing magnetic flux through a coil produces an induced potential difference. A steady magnet beside a stationary coil does not provide a continuing induced voltage merely because a field exists.
keyIdeas: Magnetic effects arise from magnets and electric currents.
Reversing current reverses the coil’s field direction.
Induction responds to change, not simply to the presence of a field.

definitions.meaning: A field describing magnetic influence at positions in space.
A magnet produced by electric current, often using a coil and magnetic core.
A measure of magnetic field passing through a surface, accounting for its area and orientation.

method: Identify whether the situation concerns a steady field, a force or induction.
State the current or magnet direction and what changes.
Use the appropriate qualitative relationship.
Explain the energy source instead of assuming a magnet creates energy.

workedExample.prompt: A bar magnet is pushed towards a stationary coil connected to a sensitive meter, held still, then pulled away. Describe the idealised meter response.
steps: During approach, the magnetic flux through the coil changes and the meter deflects.
While the magnet is held still, the flux is steady and the induced signal returns to zero.
During withdrawal, the flux changes in the opposite sense and the meter deflects oppositely.
workedExample.conclusion: The induced response depends on motion changing flux. The energy transferred during induction comes from the work done moving the magnet, not from an unlimited magnetic energy source.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming a stationary magnet always induces a current in a nearby coil.
misconceptions.correction: A continuing induced voltage requires changing flux linkage; current also requires a closed conducting path.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying only permanent magnets can produce fields.
misconceptions.correction: Electric currents also generate magnetic fields.

practice.prompt: Describe the field direction outside a bar magnet and how a small compass responds.
solution: Outside the magnet the field points from north towards south.
The compass’s north-seeking end aligns along the local field direction.

practice.prompt: A coil’s supply connections are reversed while its geometry remains fixed. Explain the effect on its magnetic poles and whether this alone determines field strength.
solution: Current reverses, so the coil’s north and south poles swap.
The field magnitude depends on current magnitude, turns and core; reversing connections alone does not specify a magnitude change.

practice.prompt: A learner proposes generating a continuous voltage by holding a magnet still inside a stationary coil. Evaluate the proposal and suggest a change that would produce an induced signal.
solution: Once stationary, the magnet produces steady flux through the coil, so no continuing induced voltage is expected.
Move the magnet relative to the coil or rotate the coil relative to the field to change flux.
Mechanical work supplies the energy; a closed circuit is needed for an induced current.

practice.prompt: A motor conductor feels a leftward force. The magnetic field reverses while current is unchanged. Predict and explain the new force direction.
solution: The force becomes rightward.
Reversing the field alone reverses the interaction force for the unchanged current.

practice.prompt: Plan a fair classroom comparison of coil turn count and magnetic strength using teacher-approved equipment.
hints: Choose one measurable response at a fixed position.
solution: Compare several turn counts at the same current and core geometry; measure field with the same sensor position.
Repeat each setting and monitor heating; different current or sensor distance would confound the comparison.

checklist: I distinguish field direction and strength.
I account for the energy source.

notes.title: Direction changes in motor action
paragraphs: An electromagnet links electrical current to a magnetic field. Increasing current or adding coil turns can strengthen the field for the same geometry, although real cores can saturate and heating constrains equipment. A motor uses force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Reversing either the current or the external field reverses that force; reversing both restores its original direction. An investigation must separate these variables. Field diagrams use arrows for direction and relative line density for strength, while remaining models rather than pictures of physical strands.

workedExamples.prompt: A conductor experiences an upward motor force. Predict the direction after reversing current only, then after reversing both current and magnetic field.
steps: Reversing current alone changes the force to downward.
Reversing both changes the force direction twice, restoring upward force.
workedExamples.conclusion: The comparison assumes the conductor remains perpendicular to the field and magnitudes are unchanged.

flashcards.front: What creates an electromagnet’s field?
flashcards.back: Electric current in its coil.

flashcards.front: What happens when only motor current reverses?
flashcards.back: The magnetic force reverses.

flashcards.front: What if current and external field both reverse?
flashcards.back: The force direction is restored.

flashcards.front: Why compare coils at controlled current?
flashcards.back: Different currents would confound the effect of turn count.

diagrams.title: Direction changes in motor action
diagrams.description: Each single reversal reverses the force.

lessons.summary: Distinguish temperature from internal energy and calculate heating or phase-change energy under stated assumptions.
objectives: Explain heating as energy transfer driven by a temperature difference.
Use E = mcΔT for a single phase.
Distinguish temperature change from a change of state.
explanation: Temperature describes a thermal condition related to particle motion, whereas internal energy includes microscopic kinetic and potential contributions across the material. A large cooler sample can have more internal energy than a small hotter sample, so temperature alone does not specify the total. Energy transferred because of a temperature difference is heating, not a substance stored inside an object.

For a material remaining in one phase with approximately constant specific heat capacity, E = mcΔT. During an ideal phase change at constant pressure, energy can change particle arrangement without raising temperature; E = mL describes that transfer using a stated specific latent heat. Real heating experiments also transfer energy to the container and surroundings, which must be included or explicitly neglected.
keyIdeas: A temperature change in °C has the same numerical size as the change in kelvins.
Specific heat capacity depends on the material and conditions.
A flat section of an ideal heating curve can represent a phase change.

definitions.meaning: The sum of microscopic kinetic and potential energies within a system.
Energy required per kilogram per degree of temperature rise under stated conditions.
Energy transferred per kilogram in a specified change of state without temperature change.

method: Identify the material, mass and whether its phase changes.
Calculate the temperature difference rather than using the final temperature alone.
Choose mcΔT or mL for each stage.
State losses and container heating assumptions, then check units.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the energy to warm 0.5 kg of liquid water from 20°C to 35°C. Use c = 4200 J/(kg °C), with no evaporation or losses.
workedExample.conclusion: The water gains 31,500 J in the stated model. A heater would generally supply more energy because the container and surroundings also receive energy.

misconceptions.mistake: Using the final temperature as ΔT.
misconceptions.correction: Subtract initial temperature from final temperature.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming energy transfer always raises temperature.
misconceptions.correction: During a phase change, energy can alter particle arrangement at constant temperature.

practice.prompt: A 2 kg solid with c = 500 J/(kg °C) warms by 8°C without changing phase. Find its energy gain.
Melting 0.2 kg of ice already at its melting temperature requires L = 334,000 J/kg. Find the required energy and explain why mcΔT is not the relevant step.
hints: This question asks only about the phase-change stage.
solution: The melting stage occurs without a temperature rise in the ideal model, but still needs energy to change particle arrangement.
successCriteria: Explains non-zero energy at constant temperature

practice.prompt: A heater supplies 12,000 J to a 1 kg sample that warms by 10°C. A student reports c = 1200 J/(kg °C). Explain how unaccounted energy loss affects this estimate.
hints: Compare supplied energy with energy actually gained by the sample.
solution: The calculation 12,000/(1 × 10) = 1200 assumes all supplied energy heats the sample.
If some energy heats the container or surroundings, the sample receives less than 12,000 J.
Using the full input therefore overestimates the sample’s specific heat capacity under these assumptions.

practice.prompt: Explain why thermal radiation can transfer energy from the Sun across space while sound cannot propagate through the same vacuum.
hints: Ask whether material particles are required.
solution: Thermal radiation is electromagnetic and can propagate through vacuum.
Sound is a mechanical disturbance requiring a material medium, which vacuum lacks.

practice.prompt: Design a fair comparison of two insulating sleeves around identical cups of warm water.
hints: Keep the stored thermal energy initially comparable.
solution: Use equal water masses and starting temperatures, identical cups and lids, and the same surroundings.
Measure temperature at the same intervals with calibrated sensors and repeat the comparison.

checklist: I separate heating and phase-change stages.
I account for losses and the container.

notes.title: Cooling has several pathways
paragraphs: Thermal transfer can occur through conduction, convection and radiation. In conduction, energy passes through a material without a bulk flow of the material. Convection involves bulk movement of a fluid and often arises when density differences occur in a gravitational field. Radiation transfers energy through electromagnetic waves and does not need a material medium. Insulation slows transfers but does not generate energy or prevent every transfer indefinitely. A comparison should keep starting temperature, exposed area, time and surroundings consistent so that any observed cooling difference can reasonably be linked to the tested feature.

workedExamples.prompt: Identical cups hold equal masses of water at the same initial temperature. One has a lid. Explain why it may cool more slowly.
steps: The lid reduces evaporation and movement of warm moist air from the water surface.
Energy can still transfer through cup walls, the lid and radiation.
workedExamples.conclusion: The lid changes transfer pathways; it does not create heat or guarantee constant temperature.

flashcards.front: Which thermal transfer needs no material medium?
flashcards.back: Radiation.

flashcards.front: What moves in convection?
flashcards.back: The fluid itself moves in bulk.

flashcards.front: Does insulation create thermal energy?
flashcards.back: No; it reduces transfer rates.

flashcards.front: Why use equal water masses in a cooling comparison?
flashcards.back: Different masses change energy needed for the same temperature change.

diagrams.title: Cooling has several pathways
diagrams.description: Covering one route leaves others active.
