nodes.detail: Evaporation and convection reduced by lid

nodes.label: Other transfer
nodes.detail: Walls and radiation still transfer energy

lessons.summary: Use particle counts to distinguish atoms, ions and isotopes, and interpret half-life as a population-level decay model.
objectives: Determine proton, neutron and electron counts.
Distinguish ionisation from nuclear change.
Calculate the remaining fraction after whole half-lives.
explanation: An atom has a small nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons outside it. Atomic number counts protons; mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count. A neutral atom has equal proton and electron counts. Gaining or losing electrons changes its charge but does not, by itself, change its nucleus or isotope.

Some nuclei change spontaneously by radioactive decay. The decay time of an individual nucleus is not predictable from a half-life. For a large population of identical unstable nuclei, half-life is the time over which the expected undecayed population halves. Repeated half-lives multiply the remaining fraction by one-half; they do not subtract the same original number each time. Activity is the decay rate and follows the same fraction under this simple model.
keyIdeas: Proton count identifies the element.
Electron changes and nuclear changes are different processes.
A half-life describes statistical behaviour, not a countdown for each nucleus.

definitions.meaning: The number of protons in a nucleus.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
The time for the expected undecayed population, or activity, of one radioactive species to fall by half.

method: Identify whether the question concerns electrons or the nucleus.
Use neutron count = mass number - atomic number.
For decay, divide elapsed time by the stated half-life.
Apply repeated halving and describe the statistical assumption.

workedExample.prompt: A large sample initially contains 6400 unstable nuclei with a half-life of 3 hours. Find the expected number remaining after 9 hours.
workedExample.conclusion: The model predicts 800 undecayed nuclei on average. An actual count can fluctuate; this does not specify which nuclei will decay or certify a material as safe.

misconceptions.mistake: Changing the neutron count when an atom loses an electron.
misconceptions.correction: Ionisation changes the electron count; neutron count belongs to the nucleus.

misconceptions.mistake: Subtracting half the original sample after every half-life.
misconceptions.correction: Halve the amount remaining at each step.

practice.prompt: A neutral atom has atomic number 8 and mass number 18. State its proton, neutron and electron counts.
solution: Protons = 8.
Neutrons = 18 - 8 = 10.
Electrons = 8 because the atom is neutral.

practice.prompt: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. It loses one of its original 11 electrons. State the ion charge and whether its mass number changes.
solution: It now has 10 electrons and 11 protons, giving charge +1 in elementary-charge units.
Mass number remains 11 + 12 = 23 because the nucleus has not changed.

practice.prompt: A background-corrected detector count rate falls from 960 counts/min to 120 counts/min in 12 hours. Assuming one radioactive species and unchanged detector conditions, find its half-life.
hints: Count how many halvings give the measured ratio.
solution: 960 → 480 → 240 → 120 is three half-lives.
Half-life = 12/3 = 4 hours.
This estimate depends on background correction, unchanged detection efficiency and the single-species model.

practice.prompt: A raw rate is 140 counts/min and background is 20 counts/min. Find the expected raw rate after two half-lives with unchanged background.
hints: Add it back after two halvings.
solution: Source rate initially = 120 counts/min; after two half-lives it is 30.
Expected raw rate = 30 + 20 = 50 counts/min.

practice.prompt: A learner says every nucleus in a sample must decay exactly one half-life after the sample was obtained. Evaluate the claim.
hints: Distinguish individual random events from population behaviour.
solution: Individual decay times are random and are not scheduled at the half-life.
For a large population, the expected undecayed number halves over that interval; some nuclei remain afterwards.

checklist: I distinguish proton, neutron and electron counts.
I identify whether charge or nucleus changes.
I state what the statistical model does and does not predict.

notes.title: Background-corrected decay
paragraphs: Background radiation contributes to a detector reading even when the source being studied is absent. Subtract a measured background rate before comparing a source’s decay. Keep detector position, measurement duration and geometry consistent. Counts fluctuate because decay is random, so a longer counting interval can provide a more stable rate estimate. A half-life applies to the expected number of unstable nuclei, or to activity for a single unchanged radioactive population. It does not establish a precise decay time for each nucleus or measure the chemical mass of all material in the sample.

workedExamples.prompt: A detector records 210 counts/min near a source and 30 counts/min as background. After one half-life, predict the total measured rate under unchanged conditions.
steps: After one half-life, source rate = 90 counts/min; adding background gives 120 counts/min.
workedExamples.conclusion: Halving the raw total to 105 would incorrectly halve the background contribution too.

flashcards.front: Why subtract background?
flashcards.back: To isolate the rate attributable to the source.

flashcards.front: Does background halve with the studied source?
flashcards.back: Not under the unchanged-background assumption.

flashcards.front: Why do repeat counts vary?
flashcards.back: Radioactive decay is random.

flashcards.front: What remains unchanged in isotopes of one element?
flashcards.back: Proton number.

diagrams.title: Background-corrected decay
diagrams.description: Only the isolated source contribution is halved.

lessons.summary: Turn a physics question into a controlled, repeatable measurement plan with a clear analysis and limitations.
objectives: Identify independent, dependent and controlled variables.
Choose a useful range and repeated measurements.
Connect a limitation to a specific improvement.
explanation: An experiment is organised around a question, not around collecting as many numbers as possible. State what you will change and how the response will be measured. Other influences that could change the response need to be controlled, monitored or acknowledged. A control variable is not the same thing as a comparison group, and some useful experiments need no separate control group.

Choose several values spanning a sensible range, with repeated measurements at each setting. Repeats help reveal variation but do not remove a shared bias such as a miscalibrated instrument. Decide the graph and comparison before inspecting the results, retain unexpected observations and document any excluded recording error. A valid conclusion must remain within the conditions and measurement quality actually tested.
keyIdeas: Operational definitions specify how quantities are measured.
Repeats and a range of settings serve different purposes.
A specific improvement addresses an identified limitation.

definitions.meaning: The quantity deliberately changed to examine its effect.
The response measured using a stated method.
A relevant quantity kept consistent so it does not obscure the intended comparison.

method: Write a measurable question and define the variables.
Choose suitable equipment, range and safe conditions.
Plan repeats, controls and a consistent recording table.
Specify the analysis and how uncertainty will limit the conclusion.

workedExample.prompt: Plan a classroom investigation of how release height affects a toy trolley’s speed at the bottom of a fixed ramp.
steps: Change release height and measure bottom speed with the same timing method.
Keep trolley mass, ramp surface and measurement position fixed; release without an extra push.
Use several teacher-approved low heights and repeat each setting, recording all readings.
Plot speed against height, or speed squared against height if testing the energy-model prediction.
workedExample.conclusion: The plan tests a defined relationship. Friction, release consistency and timing uncertainty must be considered before claiming agreement with an ideal energy model.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling extra repeats a solution to every error.
misconceptions.correction: Repeats describe variation; calibration or redesigned measurement is needed for systematic bias.

misconceptions.mistake: Deleting a point because it spoils the graph.
misconceptions.correction: Retain it unless a documented error justifies exclusion, and explain the decision.

practice.prompt: In a test of how a spring’s extension depends on applied load, identify the independent and dependent variables and one control.
hints: Distinguish what is changed from what is measured.
solution: Independent: applied load.
Dependent: extension from the unloaded length.
A control is using the same spring within its elastic range.

practice.prompt: A student measures one trolley journey at each of only two heights. Explain two changes that would improve the evidence for the shape of the speed-height relationship.
hints: Separate repeatability from the range of comparisons.
solution: Use more heights across the allowed range to examine curvature or departures from a straight line.
Repeat each height to estimate measurement variation and identify inconsistent releases.
Keep the timing method and other relevant conditions consistent.

practice.prompt: Every reading from a length sensor is 2 cm too large. A learner proposes taking 20 readings and averaging them to remove the error. Evaluate and improve the proposal.
hints: The same offset affects all readings.
solution: Averaging may reduce random variation but the +2 cm offset remains.
Check the sensor against a known reference, correct the calibration or apply a documented offset correction.
Recheck at several reference lengths to see whether the error is a constant offset or changes with length.

practice.prompt: Plan an investigation of pendulum period against string length using small swings and teacher-approved apparatus.
hints: Time several swings rather than one.
Keep release angle and bob properties controlled.
solution: Use several lengths, measure pivot-to-bob-centre distance, and time ten complete swings at each length.
Repeat and divide total time by ten; keep small release angle and the same bob.

practice.prompt: A lamp is tested at increasing settings as its battery steadily discharges. Explain a confound and one useful improvement.
solution: Later settings coincide with a weaker supply, so their effect is mixed with battery change.
Monitor actual voltage and use a stable supply or randomised repeated settings to assess drift.

checklist: My controls match plausible competing influences.
I plan a range and repeats.
My improvement addresses a named limitation.

notes.title: Temperature can confound a resistor test
paragraphs: A fair comparison needs a measurement definition that another group could repeat. “Brightness” or “strength” is too vague unless an instrument, position and unit are specified. Randomising the order of settings can reduce confounding from gradual warming or battery depletion. Repeat measurements at each setting, not only at the beginning and end. Calibration checks address systematic offsets that repetition cannot remove. Record practical limits and preserve unexpected observations so that the conclusion describes the evidence actually collected, rather than only the measurements that fit an anticipated trend.

workedExamples.prompt: Plan a low-voltage investigation of current against potential difference for a resistor.
steps: Vary the supply across several teacher-approved values; measure current and voltage across the same resistor.
Repeat readings, control temperature or allow cooling, and vary the setting order to detect warming effects.
workedExamples.conclusion: A V–I plot can test constant resistance within the measured range; a changing slope may reflect heating.

flashcards.front: What is an operational definition?
flashcards.back: A precise statement of how a variable is measured.

flashcards.front: Why randomise setting order?
flashcards.back: To reduce confounding by gradual changes over time.

flashcards.front: Do repeats remove calibration bias?
flashcards.back: No; calibration needs a separate check.

flashcards.front: Why retain unexpected readings?
flashcards.back: They may reveal variability or a genuine limitation.

diagrams.title: Temperature can confound a resistor test
diagrams.description: An unwanted pathway can change the measured response.

edges.label: more energy transfer can warm it

lessons.summary: Turn recorded measurements into a supported comparison while preserving variation, units and unexpected observations.
objectives: Calculate and interpret a mean from repeated measurements.
Compare observations with a stated relationship.
Distinguish a descriptive trend from a causal conclusion.
explanation: Keep raw readings with their units and measurement conditions before calculating summaries. A mean can describe the centre of repeated readings at one setting, but it does not show their spread. Report a suitable spread or uncertainty alongside it. Different settings should not be averaged together when the purpose is to investigate how a response changes with the independent variable.

A graph makes a proposed relationship testable. Look for the overall pattern and departures from it, then relate the evidence to the physical model. A line that looks straight is not sufficient evidence of direct proportion unless the intercept is also consistent with zero. An unexpected point is a reason to investigate recording, conditions and variation; it is not automatic permission to delete evidence.
keyIdeas: Raw data and processed summaries answer different questions.
A gradient has units determined by both axes.
Association alone does not isolate a cause.

definitions.meaning: The sum of a set of values divided by the number of values.
An observed value minus the value predicted by a stated model.
A relationship y = kx with constant ratio y/x and zero intercept.

method: Check labels, units and recording consistency without erasing raw data.
Summarise repeats at each setting and retain a measure of variation.
Plot the response against the independent variable and compare with a stated model.
Explain departures and limit the conclusion to the tested range and conditions.

workedExample.prompt: A trolley travels the same 2.0 m path in 1.8 s, 2.0 s and 2.2 s. Summarise the times and calculate 2.0 m divided by the mean time. Is this exactly the same as the mean of the three speeds?
steps: Mean time = (1.8 + 2.0 + 2.2)/3 = 2.0 s; the time range is 0.4 s.
Distance divided by mean time = 2.0/2.0 = 1.0 m/s.
Individual speeds are approximately 1.111, 1.000 and 0.909 m/s; their mean is approximately 1.007 m/s.
workedExample.conclusion: Averaging and taking a reciprocal do not generally commute. State which summary you calculated rather than labelling both procedures as the same mean speed.

misconceptions.mistake: Reporting a mean as if it contains all information about the readings.
misconceptions.correction: Include variation and retain the original observations.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling every straight graph direct proportion.
misconceptions.correction: Check whether its intercept is consistent with zero as well as whether its gradient is constant.

practice.prompt: Three repeat extension readings at one load are 4.1 cm, 4.3 cm and 4.2 cm. Find the mean and range.
hints: The range is the maximum minus minimum.

practice.prompt: An idealised graph follows extension e = 2F + 1, where e is in cm and load F is in N. Is extension directly proportional to load? Interpret the gradient and intercept.
hints: Compare the equation with y = kx.
solution: The gradient is 2 cm/N, so each additional newton increases extension by 2 cm in this model.
The intercept is 1 cm at zero load.
It is not direct proportion because the intercept is not zero; a reference offset is one possible explanation to investigate.

practice.prompt: A model predicts a period of 1.5 s. Repeated measurements are 1.4 s, 1.5 s, 1.6 s and 2.5 s. Explain how to handle the last reading and whether deleting it solely to improve agreement is justified.
hints: Separate an unusual value from an established recording error.
solution: Retain and flag the 2.5 s reading while checking notes, timing and conditions.
Repeat the measurement where possible and document any evidence of a recording or procedural error.
Do not delete it solely because it disagrees; report how inclusion affects the summary and qualify any model comparison.

practice.prompt: A model predicts 4.0, 6.0 and 8.0 cm. Measurements are 4.2, 5.8 and 8.1 cm. Find the three residuals.
solution: Residuals are 4.2 − 4.0 = +0.2 cm and 5.8 − 6.0 = −0.2 cm.
The last residual is 8.1 − 8.0 = +0.1 cm.

practice.prompt: A straight fitted graph of mass against volume has gradient 2.7 g/cm³ and non-zero intercept 5 g. Interpret both features.
hints: Gradient uses mass change per volume change.
Ask what the model predicts at zero sample volume.
solution: The gradient estimates density as 2.7 g/cm³ for the material.
The 5 g intercept could reflect an unremoved container mass or offset; it needs investigation rather than being called sample density.

checklist: I report variation as well as a mean.
I interpret gradient and intercept with units.

notes.title: Gradient connects graph and model
paragraphs: A best-fit line represents an overall trend rather than joining every measured point. Its gradient should be calculated using well-separated points on the fitted line, which need not be original observations. The intercept has the units of the vertical axis and can reveal a baseline offset. Residuals show how each observation differs from a prediction. Random scatter around zero is different from a curved residual pattern, which can indicate a poor model choice. The data range and uncertainty determine how strongly the model is supported.

workedExamples.prompt: A fitted force–extension relation passes through (0.02 m, 4 N) and (0.08 m, 16 N). Find its gradient and interpret it.
steps: For a linear spring model, this gradient is the spring constant.
workedExamples.conclusion: The relation supports k ≈ 200 N/m over the measured range, not necessarily beyond the elastic limit.

flashcards.front: Where should gradient points be chosen?
flashcards.back: Well apart on the fitted line.

flashcards.front: What are force–extension gradient units?
flashcards.back: N/m.

flashcards.front: What is a residual?
flashcards.back: Observed value minus predicted value.

flashcards.front: What can curved residuals indicate?
flashcards.back: A straight-line model may miss the relationship’s shape.

diagrams.title: Gradient connects graph and model
diagrams.description: Axis quantities determine the gradient’s meaning.

edges.label: divide force change by extension change

lessons.summary: Describe the limits of a measurement and distinguish resolution, repeated variation and systematic bias.
objectives: State a reading with a justified uncertainty convention.
Calculate a fractional or percentage uncertainty.
Explain why precision does not guarantee accuracy.
explanation: Every reported measurement has limits. Instrument resolution is the smallest displayed step or scale division; it is one contributor to uncertainty, not a universal rule for the total uncertainty. Readability, calibration, repeatability and the measurement method also matter. For classroom calculations, a question may specify a convention such as half a scale division; state that assumption rather than presenting it as valid for every instrument.

Closely grouped repeats indicate good precision under those conditions. They can still share a systematic offset and therefore be inaccurate. An uncertainty interval communicates a plausible range under the stated method, not a guarantee that the true value lies inside it. Absolute uncertainty has the measurement’s units; fractional uncertainty compares its size with the measured value, and multiplying that fraction by 100 gives a percentage.
keyIdeas: Uncertainty and a known mistake are different.
A systematic offset can survive averaging.
Keep enough digits during working and round the final report consistently.

definitions.meaning: The smallest change distinguishable on an instrument’s scale or display.
How closely repeated measurements agree under specified conditions.
A stated estimate of measurement uncertainty expressed in the same units as the quantity.

method: Identify the instrument and measurement procedure.
State the source and convention for the uncertainty estimate.
Calculate fractional uncertainty as absolute uncertainty divided by the magnitude of the measured value.
Report units, sensible rounding and limitations of the estimate.

workedExample.prompt: A length is reported as 20.0 ± 0.2 cm using a stated classroom uncertainty estimate. Give the indicated interval and percentage uncertainty.
steps: Lower endpoint = 20.0 - 0.2 = 19.8 cm; upper endpoint = 20.0 + 0.2 = 20.2 cm.
workedExample.conclusion: The report indicates 19.8 to 20.2 cm under the chosen estimate, with 1% uncertainty. It does not prove that calibration bias or all other effects have been captured.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a reading accurate because many decimal places are displayed.
misconceptions.correction: Display resolution alone does not establish calibration or accuracy.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating uncertainty as a reason to erase an awkward result.
misconceptions.correction: Report the estimate and investigate the result; uncertainty is part of the evidence.

practice.prompt: A mass is reported as 50.0 ± 0.5 g. State the indicated interval and percentage uncertainty.
hints: Divide 0.5 by 50.0 before converting to a percentage.
solution: The interval is 49.5 to 50.5 g.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.5/50.0 × 100% = 1%.

practice.prompt: Measurements A and B are 10.0 ± 0.2 cm and 40.0 ± 0.2 cm. Compare absolute and percentage uncertainties.
hints: The same absolute uncertainty need not be the same proportion.
solution: Both have absolute uncertainty 0.2 cm.
B has the smaller relative uncertainty under the stated estimates.

practice.prompt: A balance repeatedly reads 102.0 g for a reference mass known to be 100.0 g. The repeats differ by only 0.1 g. Evaluate the claim that the balance is accurate because it is precise.
solution: The small spread supports good repeatability, or precision, for this test.
The readings show an approximately +2.0 g offset from the reference, so precision does not establish accuracy.
Check calibration and other reference masses before correcting subsequent readings; one reference does not establish performance over the entire range.

practice.prompt: A measured change is 3.0 ± 0.3 cm. Calculate its percentage uncertainty.
solution: Fractional uncertainty = 0.3/3.0 = 0.1.
Percentage uncertainty = 10%.

practice.prompt: Using interval bounds, A = 12.0 ± 0.2 s and B = 12.3 ± 0.2 s. Can their indicated intervals overlap? Explain.
hints: Write each lower and upper endpoint.
Compare the intervals, not just their central values.
solution: A spans 11.8–12.2 s and B spans 12.1–12.5 s.
They overlap from 12.1 to 12.2 s, so central values alone do not establish a resolved difference under this criterion.

checklist: I use matching units in a ratio.
I distinguish spread from systematic offset.
I avoid claiming an interval is a guarantee.

notes.title: Subtracting two uncertain readings
paragraphs: An uncertainty in a difference can be larger than the uncertainty in either reading alone. Under a conservative classroom interval method, take the largest possible difference and the smallest possible difference from the endpoint intervals. A small measured change may therefore have a large percentage uncertainty even when the instrument readings look precise. State the rule being used; different statistical methods answer different questions. Repeating the same procedure can reduce random variability, but it cannot recover information lost through a coarse instrument scale or a shared calibration error.

workedExamples.prompt: A ruler reading changes from 2.0 ± 0.1 cm to 7.0 ± 0.1 cm. Use conservative endpoint bounds to report the change.
workedExamples.conclusion: The difference is 5.0 ± 0.2 cm under the stated interval method.

flashcards.front: Why can a difference have two uncertainty contributions?
flashcards.back: Both the initial and final readings have limits.

flashcards.front: What is percentage uncertainty?
flashcards.back: Absolute uncertainty divided by magnitude, multiplied by 100%.

flashcards.front: Does a narrow spread guarantee accuracy?
flashcards.back: No; a common systematic offset can remain.

flashcards.front: Why state the uncertainty convention?
flashcards.back: Different methods produce different kinds of bounds or estimates.

lessons.summary: Interpret the gradient, area and sign of a physics graph by referring to the quantities on its axes.
objectives: Find a gradient using two well-separated points.
Interpret signed area beneath a velocity-time graph.
Distinguish graph height from gradient and physical path.
explanation: Start with the axis labels and units. A gradient is change in the vertical quantity divided by change in the horizontal quantity; it is not simply the height of a point. On a displacement-time graph it represents velocity. On a velocity-time graph it represents acceleration. A straight line on either graph describes a constant gradient, but the physical meaning differs because the vertical quantities differ.

Area also gets its meaning from the axes. The signed area beneath a velocity-time graph gives displacement because velocity multiplied by time has units of length. Areas below the time axis count negatively. Total distance is found from the area beneath a speed-time graph, or by adding the magnitudes of separate signed areas. A graph describes relationships between measured quantities; it need not resemble the object’s route through space.
keyIdeas: Label both axes before interpreting a shape.
Gradient units are vertical units divided by horizontal units.
Signed displacement can be zero while distance is positive.

definitions.meaning: The change in the vertical quantity divided by the corresponding change in the horizontal quantity.
Area counted positively above an axis and negatively below it.
A line sharing a curve’s local direction at a specified point, used to estimate its instantaneous gradient.

method: Read the quantities, units and scale on each axis.
Decide whether the question needs height, gradient or area.
Use a large gradient triangle or divide areas into clear shapes.
Attach units and interpret signs in the stated physical context.

workedExample.prompt: An object moves at +3 m/s for 4 s, then at -2 m/s for 3 s. Treat the change of velocity as instantaneous for this graph model. Find displacement and distance.
workedExample.conclusion: The object finishes 6 m in the positive direction from its start but travels 18 m. The instantaneous velocity change is a simplifying model, not a physically finite acceleration.

misconceptions.mistake: Reading the height of a velocity-time point as acceleration.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph.

misconceptions.mistake: Subtracting backward travel when calculating total distance.
misconceptions.correction: Add the magnitudes of each travelled segment; signed addition gives displacement.

practice.prompt: A straight displacement-time graph passes through (2 s, 5 m) and (6 s, 17 m). Find the velocity.
Velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 s. Find the acceleration and displacement during this interval.
hints: Gradient gives acceleration; the triangular area gives displacement.
solution: Acceleration = (8 - 0)/4 = 2 m/s².
Displacement = ½ × 4 × 8 = 16 m.

practice.prompt: A velocity-time graph shows +2 m/s for 3 s followed by -3 m/s for 2 s. A learner says the object did not move because the total signed area is zero. Evaluate the statement.
hints: Compare signed area with total area magnitude.
solution: The signed areas are +6 m and -6 m, so displacement is zero.
The total distance is 6 + 6 = 12 m.
The object moved and returned to its starting position; zero displacement does not mean no motion.

practice.prompt: A constant +6 N force acts for 3 s. Calculate the force–time area and name its physical meaning.
solution: Area = 6 × 3 = +18 N s.
This is an impulse of +18 N s, equal to the change in momentum.

practice.prompt: A triangular force–displacement graph has base 0.4 m and height 50 N, with force along displacement. Find its area and explain why it is not an impulse.
hints: Compare N m with N s.
solution: It represents work because the horizontal axis is displacement; impulse requires a time axis.

checklist: I read axis labels and units.
I choose height, gradient or area deliberately.
I use signed areas for displacement.
I distinguish a graph from a physical route.

notes.title: Axes determine the meaning of area
paragraphs: Graph areas and gradients inherit units from their axes, so they cannot be interpreted by shape alone. An area under force against displacement has units N m and represents work when the plotted force is the component along motion. An area under force against time has units N s and represents impulse. A triangle is half its base times its height, but the physical meaning depends on what base and height measure. Negative regions contribute with signs, and the chosen positive direction must be stated before interpreting the result.

workedExamples.prompt: A force–time graph forms a triangle from zero force at 0 s to 10 N at 2 s and back to zero at 4 s. Find impulse.
steps: Area = ½ × 4 s × 10 N = 20 N s.
Impulse is the signed force–time area, so the momentum change is +20 kg m/s if the force is positive.
workedExamples.conclusion: The graph gives momentum change, not work; displacement information is absent.

flashcards.front: What is force–time area?
flashcards.back: Impulse, in N s.

flashcards.front: What is force–displacement area?
flashcards.back: Work, in joules, for force along displacement.

flashcards.front: What is velocity–time gradient?
flashcards.back: Acceleration.

flashcards.front: Why attach units to graph area?
flashcards.back: Units identify which physical quantity the area represents.

diagrams.title: Axes determine the meaning of area
diagrams.description: An identical triangle can represent different physics.
